title: Kirtan in new places
hookLine: hymns now sound in gurdwaras on every continent, in old ragas and new voices

lines: THE SAME HYMNS KEEP TURNING UP.
cards: Before dawn in Amritsar, the kirtan at the Harmandir Sahib has already begun. In Kuala Lumpur, a few hours ahead, a group of old men in a gurdwara is singing along with a tabla.

In Nairobi, a family will sing at its own sunrise, a few hours later. And in Vancouver, still the afternoon before, a teenager practices on a harmonium with headphones on so she won't bother her little brother.
Follow the clock around the planet, and the same hymns keep turning up.

teach.b: Kirtan means singing the praise of God, and for Sikhs it means singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.
It began with Guru Nanak and his companion Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician who played the rabab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the start, the Guru's word was meant to be sung.
That's why the main body of the Guru Granth Sahib is divided first by raag, musical modes, each with its own mood and time of day, and only then, inside each raag, by author and form.
There are thirty-one main raags: some belong to dawn, some to evening, some to longing, some to joy. Over the centuries, the instruments changed.

The harmonium came to India with Europeans in the 1800s and became a familiar sound in gurdwaras. In recent decades, some musicians have gone back to the older strings: the rabab, the dilruba, the taus.
So kirtan today is both: old raags and new voices.

teach.h: ACROSS THE WORLD, ON EVERY SCREEN.
teach.b: The diaspora has carried it a long way, to gurdwaras across the world, classrooms and camps, phones and livestreams.
The kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast every day, so a grandmother in England can listen along with Amritsar at breakfast.
Children learn the tabla in the same gurdwaras where their parents learned to read Gurmukhi. And some listeners who aren't Sikh say they were drawn in before they understood a word.
The Gurus taught that the Name is sung, not only studied.
Now that song turns up everywhere.

how: Kirtan is sung in gurdwaras, usually with harmonium and tabla and sometimes with stringed instruments; the kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast daily for Sikhs around the world.

o: singing the Guru's hymns in praise of God
reading scripture aloud, with no music at all
a silent prayer repeated alone before dawn

p: played the rabab for Guru Nanak
a musical mode with its own mood

the harmonium goes back to the Gurus' time

games.q: you're compiling the Guru's hymns into one great book. how do you arrange them?
o: by raag, the musical mode they're sung in.
games.why: the Guru Granth Sahib is divided first by raag, because the Guru's word was meant to be sung.

practice: If you can, play a recording of kirtan, or the live broadcast from the Harmandir Sahib, softly; if you can't right now, remember any kirtan you've heard on this path.
Don't try to follow the words: let the sound come to you from far away, the way it reaches homes on the other side of the world. When your mind wanders, come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan. Singing the Guru's hymns — in old raags and new voices, it now sounds in gurdwaras and homes across the world.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirtan, singing God's praise; for Sikhs, singing the Guru Granth Sahib's hymns.
